paragraphs.heading: What a gas is
paragraphs.text: A gas is a state of matter with no fixed volume and no fixed shape. Like a liquid it is a fluid, but unlike a liquid it can be compressed. A pure gas is made of single atoms, as in the noble gas neon, or of molecules, as in oxygen (O₂) or carbon dioxide. Pure gases can also be mixed together, as they are in air.

paragraphs.heading: Particles far apart
paragraphs.text: What sets gases apart from liquids and solids is the huge distance between their particles. That spacing can even make some gases invisible to us. With the particles so widely spread, the forces between them are weaker than in liquids or solids. Gases also have low density and low viscosity compared with the other states, and their particles spread out until they are evenly distributed through any container.

paragraphs.heading: Forces between particles
paragraphs.text: The forces that remain come from electric attraction and repulsion. Parts of neighbouring particles with the same charge push apart, while opposite charges pull together. Molecules with polar bonds carry lasting charge imbalances, so they feel fairly strong forces, even though each molecule stays neutral overall. Non-polar molecules have only brief, random charges, and the forces these cause are called Van der Waals forces. A gas that holds permanently charged ions is called a plasma.

paragraphs.heading: Where gases sit
paragraphs.text: On the temperature scale, the gas state lies between liquid and plasma, and plasma marks its upper limit. At the very cold end lie degenerate quantum gases, which are drawing more and more attention. Dense atomic gases chilled to very low temperatures are sorted by their statistical behaviour into Bose gases and Fermi gases.

paragraphs.heading: Describing a gas
paragraphs.text: Since most gases are hard to observe directly, scientists describe them with four properties: pressure, volume, number of particles, which chemists count in moles, and temperature. Scientists including Robert Boyle, Jacques Charles, John Dalton, Amedeo Avogadro and Joseph Gay-Lussac studied these for many gases, and their work led to a formula linking them, the ideal gas law. Boyle, for instance, used a J-shaped tube and trapped gas in its closed end behind a column of mercury, which kept the amount and temperature of the gas fixed. As he added mercury and raised the pressure, the trapped gas shrank in volume.

paragraphs.heading: Where the word came from
paragraphs.text: The word gas was first used in the early 17th century by Jan Baptist van Helmont, a chemist from Brabant. He identified carbon dioxide, the first gas known other than air. His word seems to be a spelling of the Ancient Greek word chaos as it sounds in Dutch. In using it he followed an alchemical habit that goes back to Paracelsus, for whom chaos meant something like ultra-rarefied water.
